topics.title: News Feed
topics.concepts: Fan-out on write/read, ranking, caching, pagination
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design the news feed of a social network like Facebook, Instagram or LinkedIn. Users follow other users. When someone posts, their followers should see it in their home feed, newest (or most relevant) first, and scroll back through older posts.

The core problem: a feed is read far more often than posts are written, and some accounts have tens of millions of followers. Do we build each feed when a post is written, or when the feed is read?

## Requirements

**Functional**

- Publish a post (text, image links).
- Follow and unfollow users.
- View a home feed of posts from people you follow, newest first, with infinite scroll (pagination).

**Non-functional**

- Fast feed loads: under 200 ms.
- Scale: 100 million daily active users; each opens the feed about 10 times a day; 10 million new posts per day.
- New posts may take a few seconds to appear (eventual consistency is fine).
- Some users have 50 million followers.

Out of scope: comments and likes, ads, the ranking model itself, media storage and CDN details.

## 1. Clarify requirements and estimate the scale

| Question to ask | Answer we choose | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chronological or ranked? | Chronological first; ranking as a follow-up. | Simpler merge and pagination. |
| How fresh must the feed be? | A few seconds' delay is fine. | Allows asynchronous fanout. |
| Average and maximum followers? | Average 200; celebrities up to 50 million. | Decides push vs pull. |
| How far back can users scroll? | The latest ~500 posts are cached; older posts come from storage. | Bounds cache memory. |

| Quantity | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feed reads | 100M × 10 / 86,400 s | ≈ 11,600/s average, ~50k/s peak |
| New posts | 10M / 86,400 s | ≈ 115/s |
| Fanout writes (push model) | 10M posts × 200 followers | 2 billion feed inserts/day ≈ 23k/s |
| Feed cache | 100M users × 500 IDs × 8 bytes | ≈ 400 GB → a Redis cluster |

A 45-minute plan:

| Minutes | What you do |
| --- | --- |
| 0–8 | Requirements and estimates |
| 8–15 | APIs and data model |
| 15–25 | High-level design: publish path and read path |
| 25–38 | Deep dive: fanout on write vs read, celebrities |
| 38–45 | Pagination, ranking, follow-ups |

## 2. APIs and data model

```http
POST /v1/posts              { "text": "Shipped my first Spring AI app!" }   -> 201 { "postId": "p6" }
POST /v1/users/{id}/follow                                                 -> 204
GET  /v1/feed?limit=20&cursor=<opaque>                                     -> 200 { "posts": [...], "nextCursor": "..." }
```

| Store | Contents | Technology |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Posts | postId, authorId, text, mediaUrls, createdAt | Sharded SQL or Cassandra, plus a cache |
| Follow graph | (followerId, followeeId) both directions | Sharded SQL or a graph/KV store |
| Feed cache | userId → list of recent post IDs, newest first | Redis lists or sorted sets |
| Users | userId, name, avatar | SQL + cache |

**Post IDs are time-sortable** (for example Snowflake IDs: timestamp + machine + sequence). Sorting by ID then means sorting by time, which makes merging and cursors simple.

The feed cache stores **only post IDs**, not full posts. A post shared to 200 feeds is stored once; editing or deleting it does not require updating 200 copies.

## 3. High-level design

[![Selected design: the post service saves posts and emits a new-post event; fanout workers read followers from the follow graph and push the post ID into each follower's feed cache; the feed service reads IDs from the feed cache and hydrates them from the post store, adding celebrity posts on read.](designs/hld-5.svg)](designs/hld-5.svg)

**Publish path**

1. The user creates a post; the post service stores it and returns.
2. It publishes a "new post" event to a queue.
3. Fanout workers look up the author's followers and add the post ID to the front of each follower's feed list in Redis (trimming each list to 500 IDs).

**Read path**

1. The feed service reads the first 20 post IDs from the user's feed list.
2. It fetches the posts (and author names, avatars) from caches in one batch – called **hydration**.
3. It returns them with a cursor for the next page.

[![Feed read path: the feed service reads post IDs from the user's precomputed feed list, merges recent posts from followed celebrities, fetches post bodies and author details in one batch, filters deleted or hidden posts, and returns a page with a cursor.](learning-figures/hld-5-read.svg)](learning-figures/hld-5-read.svg)

## 4. Deep dive: the fanout algorithm – on write vs on read

| | **Fanout on write (push)** | **Fanout on read (pull)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When work happens | When a post is created: copy its ID into every follower's feed | When a feed is opened: fetch recent posts from everyone you follow and merge |
| Feed read | Very fast – feed is precomputed | Slow – one query per followee, then merge |
| Write cost | High for authors with many followers | Cheap |
| Wasted work | Inactive users' feeds are updated anyway | None |
| Problem case | A celebrity post means 50 million inserts | A user following 2,000 accounts |

**Use a hybrid**, as large social networks describe doing:

- **Normal authors** (say, under 10,000 followers): fanout on write.
- **Celebrities**: no fanout. Their posts are kept in their own recent-posts list.
- **On read**: take the precomputed feed, then merge in recent posts from the few celebrities the user follows, sorted by post ID.

![Animation: Asha, with 200 followers, posts and fanout workers push the post ID into each follower's feed list; a celebrity with 50 million followers posts and nothing is pushed; when Ben opens his feed, his precomputed list is merged with the celebrity's recent posts.](learning-figures/hld-5-hybrid.gif)

```java
public List<Post> getFeed(long userId, int limit, Cursor cursor) {
    List<Long> ids = new ArrayList<>(feedCache.range(userId, cursor, limit));     // pushed posts
    for (long celeb : followGraph.celebritiesFollowedBy(userId)) {
        ids.addAll(recentPosts.range(celeb, cursor, limit));                      // pulled posts
    }
    List<Long> page = ids.stream()
            .distinct()
            .sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder())        // time-sortable IDs: newest first
            .limit(limit)
            .toList();
    return postCache.getAll(page).stream()             // batch hydrate
            .filter(p -> p != null && visibility.canSee(userId, p))   // deleted or hidden posts drop out
            .toList();
}
```

**Inactive users.** Skip fanout to users who have not logged in for 30 days; when they return, build their feed by pulling (a one-time cost).

**Fanout workers** are stateless and read from a partitioned queue. A celebrity threshold keeps any single post's fanout bounded, so one post cannot clog the workers for everyone else.

## 5. Pagination, ranking and failures

**Cursor pagination, not offsets.** `?page=2` breaks when new posts arrive – the user sees duplicates as everything shifts down. Use a cursor: "give me 20 posts with ID smaller than `p17`". Because IDs are time-sorted, new posts at the top do not disturb the next page.

**Ranking.** For a ranked feed, take a few hundred candidate IDs from the same sources, score them with a model (recency, closeness to the author, engagement), and cache the ranked order for this session so scrolling is stable.

**Deletes and privacy changes.** The feed cache may still hold a deleted post's ID. Hydration checks the post store, so deleted or newly private posts are dropped at read time. That is another reason to store IDs, not copies.

**Unfollow.** Stop showing the author's posts by filtering at read time against the current follow graph; a background job can remove old IDs from the cached list later.

**Failures**

- *Fanout lag*: posts appear a few seconds late; feeds still work.
- *Redis feed shard down*: rebuild that user's feed by pulling from followees (slower, but correct).
- *Hot celebrity post*: millions of hydrations of the same post hit one cache key; replicate hot posts in a local in-process cache.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**Why not just query "posts from everyone I follow ORDER BY time" on every load?** At 50k feed loads per second, each joining hundreds of followees, the database cannot keep up. Precomputing feeds trades write work for fast reads.

**How do you choose the celebrity threshold?** Measure fanout cost. Typical answers are 10k–100k followers; it can also depend on how often the author posts.

**How big is the feed cache and can we lose it?** About 400 GB of IDs here. It is a cache – if lost, rebuild feeds by pulling. Keep replicas to avoid a slow, mass rebuild.

**How do you show a new post to its author immediately?** Insert it into the author's own feed synchronously, or merge the author's latest posts on read. Followers see it after fanout.

**What about a user who follows 5,000 people?** Fanout on write handles it well – their feed is just a list. Pull would be expensive for them, which is why push is the default.

**How would you add likes and comment counts?** Store counters separately and fetch them during hydration; they change too often to copy into feed entries.

## 7. Going deeper (optional)

The detailed version of this lesson handles feed **sessions**: freeze the sequence of candidate IDs when the user starts scrolling so pages never repeat or skip, while still checking current visibility for each post. It also shows why a page can legitimately be empty yet still return a next cursor (every candidate on it became hidden).

[![Freeze an ID sequence for a feed session: pushed and pulled posts are de-duplicated into one order; page one returns p5 and p4; a new post p6 does not shift the next page, and only a refresh starts a new session with p6 first.](learning-figures/hld-5-session.svg)](learning-figures/hld-5-session.svg)

[![An empty page still advances: after two candidates become hidden, a scan budget of two returns no items but moves the cursor forward past them.](learning-figures/hld-5-visibility.svg)](learning-figures/hld-5-visibility.svg)

[Open the news-feed walkthrough](learning-labs/news-feed.html), or read the runnable Java: [FeedEngine.java](reference-code/learning/kb/feed/FeedEngine.java), [FeedChecks.java](reference-code/learning/kb/feed/FeedChecks.java) and [FeedTrace.java](reference-code/learning/kb/feed/FeedTrace.java).

## 8. Closing answer

"Posts are stored once with time-sortable IDs. When a normal user posts, fanout workers push the post ID into each follower's feed list in Redis, trimmed to the latest 500. Celebrities are not fanned out; their recent posts are pulled and merged at read time – a hybrid that keeps both writes and reads bounded. The feed service reads IDs, merges celebrity posts, hydrates bodies and authors in one batch, filters deleted or hidden posts, and paginates with an ID cursor so new posts never shift pages. Feeds are caches: a lost feed is rebuilt by pulling, and fanout delay only makes posts appear a few seconds later."

topics.title: RAG Fundamentals
topics.concepts: Documents + chunks + embeddings + vector DB + retrieval + LLM
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Explain Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) end to end: why it exists, the ingestion pipeline (documents → chunks → embeddings → vector store) and the query pipeline (question → retrieve → augment prompt → generate with citations), with a minimal Spring AI implementation and its typical failure modes.

## Requirements

- Why RAG instead of fine-tuning for private and changing knowledge.
- Ingestion: loading, cleaning, chunking, embedding, metadata, storage.
- Query: embedding the question, top-k retrieval, prompt assembly, grounded generation.
- Citations and "I don't know" behaviour. Failure modes and how to evaluate.

## 1. Selected RAG solution

I build a private-policy assistant without retraining weights for every policy update. Ingestion parses approved revisions, chunks meaningful sections and publishes a scoped retrieval index. At query time I authenticate, retrieve permitted candidates, select evidence within budget and ask for a cited answer. The model's general knowledge is not authoritative for the private policy.

## 2. Answer contract and execution

```text
POST /ask {question,conversationId} -> {answer,citations,abstained}
Citation: sourceId,revision,chunkId
Execution: authorize -> retrieve -> pack evidence -> generate -> validate
No supporting passage -> {answer:"No approved evidence found",abstained:true}
```

Source `leave:v3:c4` caps carry-over at five days. For “May I carry seven?”, the answer is no under that passage, citing it and identifying any unavailable exception policy. It does not invent an exception. The validator rejects citations outside retrieved authorized IDs and evaluates whether passages support claims; valid IDs alone do not prove entailment.

With 6,000 evidence tokens and 500-token chunks, fewer than twelve may fit after wrappers/metadata. I reserve output and instructions before selecting evidence. Evaluation separates source recall from supported-answer rate and includes absent answers, conflicting revisions, deleted sources and forbidden tenants. A retrieval miss is not repaired by pretending a better prompt can reconstruct private facts that were never supplied.

## 3. Final design diagram

[![RAG Fundamentals: Document ingestion publishes Versioned chunks; Versioned chunks searchable evidence Scoped retrieval; Scoped retrieval selected passages Context budgeter; Context budgeter bounded prompt ChatClient; ChatClient structured claims Citation validator; Citation validator validated result Answer or abstention](designs/ai-5.svg)](designs/ai-5.svg)

An **ingestion pipeline** prepares documents. A **retriever** selects evidence. A **grounded answer** is supported by that evidence. A **citation** points to a source; merely printing a valid source ID does not prove the source supports the sentence.

## 4. Critical operation: worked execution

![A query uses published source versions from the retrieval index.](lessons/ai-5-flow.svg)

*A query uses published source versions from the retrieval index.*

![When the answer is absent, fluent completion is not a recovery method.](lessons/ai-5-failure.svg)

*When the answer is absent, fluent completion is not a recovery method.*

### Trace one answer

Source `leave-policy:v3:chunk4` says “Annual carry-over is capped at five days.” A question asks “Can I carry seven days?” A supported answer says no under that passage and cites it, while noting any missing exception policy. It must not invent an exception because seven sounds reasonable.

With 6,000 tokens available for evidence and chunks averaging 500 tokens, at most about 12 fit before citation wrappers and other overhead. Increasing top-k without budgeting can displace instructions or truncate important passages. Chunk boundaries should preserve meaning, not just count characters.

## 5. Detailed decisions, algorithms and failure behaviour

### Mechanism and rationale

**Design question:** How can an assistant answer private-document questions without training a model on every document update?

RAG retrieves relevant authorized evidence at inference time and supplies it to a generator. Ingestion and query serving are different pipelines. Retrieval errors and generation errors must be diagnosed separately; a good model cannot cite an absent or forbidden source correctly.

### Architecture and contracts

```text
Versioned source -> parse/chunk/embed -> index; question -> authorize -> retrieve/rerank -> budget context -> generate cited answer -> verify or abstain

Application contracts (design outline):
Question(tenant,user,query); Evidence(chunkId,documentVersion,passage); GroundedAnswer(text,sourceIds,abstained)
```

Use Spring AI Document, EmbeddingModel and VectorStore behind application authorization. QuestionAnswerAdvisor can provide a simple RAG path; the application still owns filtering, source versioning and answer validation.

### Worked reasoning and capacity example

A 12,000-token input allowance minus 1,000 task instructions and 2,000 conversation leaves 9,000 tokens for evidence; eight 700-token chunks use 5,600, leaving room for question and metadata. The top-k setting must obey the token budget, not just a document count.

### Java and Spring AI implementation outline

```java
record Evidence(String id, String revision, String text) {}
record GroundedAnswer(String text, java.util.List<String> sourceIds, boolean abstained) {}
// Reject citations absent from the authorized Evidence list.
// A citation ID must resolve to the exact revision used to answer.
```

### Design decisions and alternatives

I start with a lexical/vector baseline and a small golden dataset. Add query rewriting or reranking only when observed failures justify the extra call and latency. Citation output needs evidence IDs from retrieved records rather than invented URLs.

### Failure scenario and safe recovery

A top-ranked document is obsolete or includes a prompt injection. Filter by tenant, ACL and revision policy; treat source text as evidence only; preserve citations to immutable revisions so answers remain auditable.

### Security, privacy and provenance

RAG does not inherently prevent hallucination. Retrieving more chunks can increase irrelevant context and reduce answer quality.


**Verification criteria:** Measure retrieval recall, answer support, citation correctness, abstention behavior, authorization violations and freshness separately. A single similarity score cannot replace these checks.

### Further reading

- [Spring AI 1.1 ChatClient and request APIs](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/chatclient.html).
- [Spring AI tool-execution boundary](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/tools.html).
- [MCP specification, versioned protocol concepts](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18).
- [Original RAG research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) and [Transformer research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) for background rather than framework instructions.

### Work through evaluation

Measure retrieval recall separately from answer support. If the right passage was never retrieved, changing the final prompt cannot reliably repair the missing evidence. If the passage was retrieved but the answer contradicts it, generation or context construction needs attention.

Store document, chunk and revision IDs in the answer trace. On deletion or permission change, enforce current authorization at query time and remove stale index/cached evidence under the lifecycle policy. Treat retrieved text as untrusted data, including instructions embedded in documents.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**Is RAG a guarantee against hallucination?** No. Retrieval and generation can both fail.

**Does a citation ID prove support?** No. Check the cited passage actually entails the claim.

## 7. Closing answer

My RAG answer separates ingestion from query serving, retrieves only authorized current evidence, and validates the final claim-to-source relation. Missing evidence becomes an explicit answer limitation. Retrieval recall and generation support are measured separately, so failures are fixed at their actual stage.
